extracted.intended_audience: general public, municipal officials, public health authorities, and policymakers concerned with urban sanitation and nuisance abatement
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for evaluating and managing municipal nuisances (street-cleaning, garbage removal, offensive trades, sewage odors, snow removal) illustrated via comparisons between New York, Paris, and London.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of street-cleaning
rubrics_metrics.description: "Street-cleaning in cities has for its aim the removal of dust, mud, snow, filth, and household refuse.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household refuse ought to be thrown directly into the carts; regulations often conflict with rag-pickers' privileges. The statement is presented as the high-level objective against which systems should be judged (completeness in removing listed materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of workforce and mechanization
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative metrics of sweepers, machines, area to be cleaned, wages, and hours (e.g., New York employs 387 sweepers for 1,415 acres; Paris 3,180 sweepers +190 machines for 2,667 acres).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate adequacy by ratios (men per acre), presence of mechanical equipment (machines doing work of ten men), and hours worked; consider wage and hours differences when comparing capacity. The author deduces concrete outcomes (how many more men could be employed or money saved if wages differed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and budget realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of actual expenses and the limits they impose (e.g., New York street-cleaning expense 1879 was $690,000; Paris 1878 $817,000 including snow removal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments about performance must account for available appropriations and extraordinary costs (snow removal); cannot expect Paris-level results on much smaller budgets. Example: snow removal costs estimated per cubic metre with municipal councils weighing extra appropriations vs limits on spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness and responsiveness to extraordinary events (snow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations about prompt and energetic measures in snow-storms and rapid clearance of streets (criticism where slow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess agencies by speed of clearing after heavy snow, use of extra forces (military, large temporary workforce), technology (steam jets in London), pre-positioning of labor and resources. Compare time-to-clear and whether extra appropriations or manpower were authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of household refuse vs rag-pickers' privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice: in Paris the rag-picking privilege is farmed to contractors employing ~7,000 chiffoniers; in many places refuse is thrown on streets for rag-pickers to pick over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems on whether they permit refuse to be left on streets for rag-pickers (aesthetic and health prejudice) versus contracting/monopolizing collection and whether that produces municipal revenue. Consider the trade-off between rag-picker livelihoods, contractor systems, and visible nuisance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/schedule for removal of household refuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal: refuse intended for removal and thrown on the street for this purpose ought to be taken away at an early hour of the morning; often it remains till evening and is scattered about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess collection schedules (early-morning pickup vs evening accumulation) and their impact on scattering, odors, and public nuisance; evaluate enforcement of rules that would prevent evening dumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disinfectants and contractors' sanitary practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Odors from night-soil depots and sewage arise in part from the absence of disinfectants which should be used by contractors who empty cesspools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: contractors must use disinfectants and proper handling; failure and possible connivance by police/authorities should be investigated. Evaluate contractor supervision and sanitary protocols for sewage handling and night-soil depots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing nuisance (comfort) vs public-health hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission report: emanations from sewers and factory chimneys 'do not contribute, in any degree whatever, to the development or propagation of epidemic affections.' Odors may be harmless to health but destructive of comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing complaints, determine whether the problem is a discomfort/quality-of-life issue or a demonstrable public-health risk; policy responses differ (reassurance vs sanitary interventions). Document scientific/medical findings rather than solely public outcry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic necessity of offensive trades vs feasibility of banishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive trades constitute an important part of a city's industries; their banishment would strike a terrible blow at commercial prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy must weigh public-health/comfort benefits of restricting trades (meat markets, tanneries, etc.) against economic impacts and allied businesses. Evaluate alternatives (regulation, location, controls) rather than outright prohibition where commerce is vital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private responsibility and household-level sorting
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal: furnish every householder with two boxes (one for 'dry dirt' and one for 'muck'), taken away once a week, and forbid throwing refuse into the street under penalties; make householder responsible for doorstep/pavement cleanliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess systems for assigning responsibility to householders, providing source-separation containers, collection frequency, enforcement (penalties), and equity (affordability of private contracts for frequent service).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting practices, wages and supervision of scavengers/dustmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Scavenging often done by contract; men employed are underpaid, decline duties except when bribed; reports of black-mail by dustmen and neglect in poor neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contract terms, pay levels, incentives, monitoring, and fairness across neighborhoods; measure service frequency and reliability, and whether low pay results in bribery or patchy service requiring reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure condition (pavement repair) as determinant of cleanliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'The complete repair of this pavement is absolutely necessary' — poor pavements lead to puddles that trap filth and make cleaning ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pavement condition and other infrastructure (drains, sewers, alleys) in assessments of sanitation; poor infrastructure increases difficulty and cost of effective cleaning and may concentrate filth in specific areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and availability of municipal expenditure data
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty in finding municipal expenditure data for some cities (Paris has no official journal like our 'City Record'), making it hard to learn sources/amounts of revenue from refuse handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: availability of clear municipal financial records on sanitation operations is necessary for fair comparison and accountability; lack of transparency hampers evaluation and public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate technologies and methods (machines, steam, paving types)
rubrics_metrics.description: References to machines that perform work of many men, steam jets to melt snow, and different paving types (wood pavement) with trade-offs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate adoption of technology (mechanical sweepers, steam melting, pavement materials) for effectiveness, unintended consequences (e.g., wood pavement later judged a mistake), and cost-benefit given local conditions.
